content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters.
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
84:## The curator's role and decisions
85-
86-The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.
87-
88-Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.
89-
90-A decision is consequential if it:
91-
92-- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
93-- touches microGPT: a line of its two programs, its speed or its readability;
94-- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
95-- or cannot be undone.
96-
97-It reaches the curator in one of three ways:
98-
99-1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
100-2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
101-3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.
102-
103-Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.
104-
105-- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
106-- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
107-- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it.
108-- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
109-- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
110-- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
111-- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
112-- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
113-- Propose to the curator in words first a change to how the curator and you work together: what you say to the curator, the asks, the held list and the review list. Make it only after the curator approves.
114-- Make any other change to a skill yourself, and tell the curator when it lands: what changed, why, what it fixes, and any risk to watch for.
115-
116-## The facts of this environment
117-
118-- The curator reads on an iPhone, often while iOS Speak reads aloud at a fast rate, and writes by dictation.
119-- A repository path does not open on the phone. A page link does, and so does a pushed file's GitHub URL: `https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/<path>`.
120-- The curator's client can show stale state. Answer what is in flight from the tree.
121-- The curator's time zone is Central European. The container's clock is UTC.
122-- The context is compacted when it grows long. The container can be lost, and a VM restart can roll the disk back. Only what is pushed survives.
123-- The session runs in auto mode. Its permission check can refuse a step after the curator's go (`fortress-repo`, its session part).
124-- The prompt cache lives an hour for the main session and a headless session, and five minutes for a subagent.
--
151:3. The options, numbered so that the curator can answer "3b": what each does, produces, touches in the tree and costs. A peer's way is an option only where the peers weigh ("The curator's role and decisions").
152-4. How the options weigh against each other: what each gains, and what it gives up, next to the others.
153-5. Your recommendation, in one line, last, never in place of the explanation.
154-
155-Before you put a question, run every probe that it needs. Say whether the path to the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library, needs its answer. Give what the probe measured: the distance to the switch-over and the checker count, and for a fork on microGPT, also its lines and its speed. Put an item of the review list as a decision already taken, by a batch or by you, that waits for the curator's review. Never put it as a hold.
156-
157-Give each decision a default that the curator can take without reading the argument. Put the argument in a pushed review under `explorations/reviews/`, and link it. Offer no option that does nothing.
158-
159-**Quiet times.**
160-
161-- While the curator is away, keep your messages to the minimum: gather evidence and do the work. The curator is away:
162-  - after the curator has said that they are away or asleep;
163-  - in a turn that a check-in or a hook started, not a message of the curator's.
164-
165-  Send no running commentary, and no line that the curator cannot act on, such as a closing offer of queued questions. Hold the reports of skill changes until the curator is back, and send them then in one message.
166-- Do not tell the curator about edits to the record. When the curator asks you to record words, reply "noted".
167-- Say nothing about a running batch until it lands or fails, not even that it started. If the curator asks, answer from the tree. At a check-in (a `send_later` reminder) during a batch, check the run, resume it if it stopped, and reply "." alone.
168-- Answer the git-check hook's reminders silently. Never commit unready work to satisfy one.
169-- Send a push notification (the PushNotification tool) only for a long run's end, a hold or the model check's alarm. It reaches the phone only outside the app.
170-
171-**While the curator reads turn by turn,** hold the points. An answer to each point as it comes buries the curator in text.
172-
173-- Write each point on the held list, one line in your words, with the UTC time of its message.
174-- Reply with that line and "holding", in three lines at most.
175-- Answer nothing until the curator says the reading is done. Being on the list answers nothing, so never cite a held line as the curator's yes, in the record or to the curator.
176-- If the curator marks a point "now", act on it at once.
177-
178-**Pages.**
179-
180-- Send a document for approval as a page with the Artifact tool, never as a diff.
181-- The curator listens to a page with iOS Speak at a fast rate. So every page has a Select button beside each larger section's heading, which selects that section's text for Speak.
182-- Put a section's references at its bottom, numbered by point, never inside the points. The Select button leaves them out, so that Speak never reads citations.
183-- Give every page the house style: the CSS and the Select button's script of https://claude.ai/artifact/FoTnH7KzXt5MtGk3tTcZ8W, the plan's page.
184-- Write a page's glossary as a dictionary does: the term, then a noun phrase with no article.
185-- After a compaction, publish a page by its URL: a publish by source path alone makes a new page. Rebuild a lost source from the published page.
186-

content.content:
As in `reviews/batch-20-review.md`: each rung's commit, its `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md`; its section of the record and the record's review before the launch (`coordinator/climb-batch-21-review.md`, both reads); the gather's `RECORD.md`, the judge's `JUDGE-review.md` and `REPAIR-review.md`; the run's results in its journal; and the code and the specification on main. Three standards, kept apart:
- the specification;
- the team's built intent and the library's own way (P-27);
- the decisions on record: P-155, P-156 with the curator's two answers of today (question 1, option 1, `Index` outside `Object`; question 2, option 2, `atMost` under its method condition), P-157 as rewritten today to the checker branch, P-146, P-152, and the record's forks at their defaults (`CLIMB-BATCH-21.md:66-181`).

### The verdicts

- **Rung S, the symbolic operators' library fixes: in the spirit of P-155 and item 59's answer,** by the library's own device for the shape (juxtaposition's three top-level operators). One reading where walk splits with the rules: fork 5's refusal depends on walk's cache (split 4).
- **Rung X, the self type and the bounds in the exclusion test: in the spirit of P-157 as rewritten, P-146 and P-152,** in the exclusion test only (fork 30). One move beyond the record's expected ones: row 713's pair, whose recorded default was the refusal, now compiles (split 2).
- **Rung B, the index bound with the tuple rule: in the spirit of P-156 and both answers,** with two readings no decision covers (a type extending only `Index` is an `Object`; walk's exclusion as the dual), and one sentence of P-156 that its own Appendix I entry contradicts by the brief's order (split 1). Its specification work needed the merged-diff review's repair.
- **Rung N, the slices and a list's equality: in the spirit of P-27 and P-154,** the library's own way at each site (`Array1.subarray`'s offset; the maps' `Equality` entry).
- **No ruling on a rung.** Four skeptics approved, thirteen fix commits, none contested, one a defect of the change (B's void type). The merged-diff review blocked on one specification-text finding; its judge ruled repair, and the repair landed.

### Where the text, the brief or the principles split

**1. P-156's reason against rung B's Appendix I entry: the team's own fix, or the revival's departure.**
- What P-156 says: "Why: it is the team's own fix for this pair (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`), its "magic" read as subtyping" (`POSITIONS.md:67`).

# Climb batch 21

## 1. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. It runs a program without static types. The **compiled path** checks a program's types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode. The compiled path still uses its own small library, the **prelude**, until the **switch-over**, when it takes over the interpreter's library, the **one library**.
- **The distance** is the number of errors the checker reports on the one library. Each error has a **site**. **The count** is the checker's errors on the library's `FortressLibrary` component, read by the **count stage**, which also gives the checker's time.
- **The full check** is the checker's overloading check reading the symbolic operators too (`+`, `-`, `=`, `||`, the subscripts `[ ]` and the rest). Today it reads only operators named by a word of capitals, such as `MAX` (row 584); P-155 turns it on. The **shadow** is a copy of the checker with the full check on, compiled beside the build; the symbolic-operator probe measured with it.
- An **api** is a component's interface (a `.fsi` file); the **component** is its code (a `.fss` file). The **export error** is one error that lists every declaration where an api and its component differ; each declaration it lists is an **entry**.
- A **tuple** is a value such as `(1, 2)`. An array of rank 2 is indexed by a pair: `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)`.
- A **row** is an entry of the gap ledger, cited by number. An **item** is a numbered question in PLAN's list "Pavol's answers".
- A **rung** is one fix, built by one worker in its own copy of the tree and checked by a second worker, the skeptic. A **batch** is a few rungs, merged and tested together by the **gate** and landed at once. **Two runs of one record** are two batches, the second launched after the first lands, as batches 6 and 6b and 7 and 7b ran.
- **Test first.** Every fix starts with a test that shows the defect, seen failing before the edit and passing after. An **expected failure** is a test named `XXX...` that passes while the defect is there; when the fix lands it is **promoted** to a plain name. A **guard** is a test that passes before and after.

### Where the distance stands

- After climb batch 20 the distance is 5 and the count 3 ([gate](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-20/gate/distance.txt); F-53). Its five: the second export error, 43 entries; row 731's 3 (`BIG MIN` twice and `List.fss:146`); item 46's fused arm (row 632).
- With the full check on, the same library gives 191: the 5 and 186 more, three of them crashes on `AnyList`'s `||` (F-245; the planner reproduced it on this base, section 4).
- **This batch's aim is the full check on at the gate's 5.** It cannot move the 5 themselves: row 731's 3 and the fused arm are left out by the brief, and the export error stays while its `Maybe` and `String` entries do.

**Run 1, climb batch 21**, the library and walk changes that the full check needs, and two that share nothing with them:

- **S, the symbolic operators' library fixes (P-155; rows 585, 611, 784).** The probe's seven known fixes: `String`'s four concatenation operators as top-level operators, as juxtaposition's already are; `EmptyString`'s meet; `Integral`'s and `ZZ`'s `=`; `|_|` by `String`'s api header; `Maybe`'s meets; the api's six vector and matrix operators that the component lacks out; `Float`'s `^` meet. #!/bin/bash
# seed-worktree.sh <base-worktree> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
#
# Makes a worktree that is ready to compile and run Fortress without building anything, by copying the
# build and the caches of a baseline worktree that has been built once, and translating the parts of the
# caches that are keyed by the source tree's absolute path (explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md).
#
#   <base-worktree>  a clean worktree of this repository at some commit B, on which `ant compileAll` and the
#                    library-order recompile (explorations/repo-internals.md, "Compile order matters") have
#                    run, and nothing since.
#   <new-worktree>   where the new worktree goes; made by `git worktree add`, reused if it already exists.
#   <branch>         the branch it checks out: an existing local branch, else origin's, else a new branch
#                    cut from <start-point>, which defaults to B; `-` makes a detached worktree at
#                    <start-point> instead. Old-against-new runs need no copy of the base: tools/old-fortress.sh
#                    runs the base build itself with a private caches folder.
#
# What it does, in order: adds the worktree; copies ProjectFortress/build, ProjectFortress/.dependencies
# and default_repository/caches from the base; renames every file of the AST caches (analyzed_cache,
# interpreter_cache, interpreter_parsed_cache) to the hash of its source's new path (NamingCzar.deCaseName,
# compiler/NamingCzar.java:244-245; GraphNode.java:33 hashes the canonical path) and rewrites the base path
# inside it; rewrites the base path in the bytecode-cache jars' SourceFile attributes (debug information
# only: jars copied unchanged also run, but their stack traces would name the base's files); and makes the
# new worktree the base's replica in its file dates too. The copies keep the base's dates (cp -a), every
# tracked file whose content is the base's takes the base file's date, and every tracked file that differs
# from B, committed or not, is stamped later than everything copied. Dates decide three things. The
# repository uses a cached entry only when it is not older than its source (repository/GraphRepository.java:244,
# :283; a changed api also makes everything that imports it stale, :600-620). Ant regenerates the AST
# nodes, the parsers and Operators.java when an input is newer than the generated file (build.xml:371-384,
# :450-467, :1335-1400); the checkout's own dates make it regenerate them, and javac then recompiles 1,077
# files. And javac recompiles a source newer than its class (build-cache-exploration.md, section 6). So the
# next `fortress compile` of a differing library source rebuilds it, and a worktree whose ProjectFortress/src
# differs from B is seeded with a warning: the copied build is B's, so the worker runs ant compileAll, which
# recompiles the differing sources (and deletes the caches, build.xml:715 and :356), and the library-order
# recompile before its first compiled run. The base's own dates must be a build's: a base built in place by
# ant, or seeded by this script.
#
# A worktree that already has ProjectFortress/build is left alone (a relaunch keeps the worker's own build);
# SEED_FORCE=1 replaces its build and caches with the base's.
#
# Prints one line per step with its time, and the seeded worktree's path last. Exits non-zero, having

#!/bin/bash
# The distance stage with the full overloading check: the gate's distance/run.sh, with the
# shadowed OverloadingChecker (checker-shadow.py beside this script) compiled by scalac and
# put ahead of everything on the run's class path.
#
#     explorations/perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/run-shadow.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> [export] [catch]
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with the call set up as the fortress-repo skill says, after
# ant compileAll. With `export`, the export check's isDeclaredName admits symbolic names too;
# with `catch`, a checker crash on one name is printed and the check goes on (checker-shadow.py).
# The scratch directory gets the shadow source and classes, the copy of run.sh (whose one
# changed line puts $EXTRA_CP first on the java class path), and the run's own scratch
# (run.txt, errors.tsv) under <scratch-dir>/d.
set -u
OUT=${1:?usage: run-shadow.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> [export]}
SC=${2:?usage: run-shadow.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> [export]}
case "$SC" in /*) ;; *) SC="$PWD/$SC" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
P="$FH/explorations/perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2"
mkdir -p "$SC/ocsrc" "$SC/occlasses" || exit 1
rm -f "$SC"/ocsrc/*.scala
rm -rf "$SC/occlasses"/* 
python3 "$P/checker-shadow.py" "$FH" "$SC/ocsrc" "${@:3}" || exit 1
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" | tail -1)
java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -nowarn -classpath "$CP" -d "$SC/occlasses" -encoding UTF-8 \
     "$SC"/ocsrc/*.scala || { echo "run-shadow: scalac failed" >&2 ; exit 1 ; }
sed 's#-cp "\$SCRATCH/shadow-classes:#-cp "${EXTRA_CP:+$EXTRA_CP:}$SCRATCH/shadow-classes:#' \
    "$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh" > "$SC/run.sh"
grep -q 'EXTRA_CP' "$SC/run.sh" || { echo "run-shadow: run.sh's class path line moved" >&2 ; exit 1 ; }
# run.sh finds its helpers through $FORTRESS_HOME, so the copy may live anywhere
EXTRA_CP="$SC/occlasses" bash "$SC/run.sh" "$OUT" "$SC/d"

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's distance stage: the compiled checker over the whole interpreter library, the
# twelve prelude apis and their twelve components, every stage of every unit run whatever
# the earlier stages reported, so that nothing hides behind an early return; one table.
#
# Why it exists: Pavol's answer 11 (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-26): the full measurement of the
# distance to the switch-over "becomes a report-only stage of phase 3's gates, whose job is
# driving it down". The checker-count stage beside it (../checker-count/run.sh) sees only
# the errors before each api's early return, 62 of about 1,740 on 2026-09-27.
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched: the
# shadow sources and classes, the driver, the checker's caches (-Dfortress.caches) and the
# JVM's temporary directory (so Rats! leaves nothing in /tmp) go to the scratch directory
# (default: $TMPDIR or /tmp), and the caches are deleted at the end. It never removes
# /tmp/fortress*rats, which other runs on the machine use. Exit 0 if the table was
# produced, 1 if it could not be. One JVM, -Xmx4g, one busy core: 789 s on the idle 4-CPU
# container on 2026-09-27, 14 to 24 minutes under load 7 to 18 (switch-over-distance-flat.md
# section 5); the table's #seconds and #machine rows say what each run took and where.
#
# The setting: "any" by default, the compiled path with the implicit bound Any
# (DistanceMulti's -setting any: the extends-Object pre-desugaring off, as walk's, and the
# compiled-expression desugaring on, as the compile path's). Answer 11 names the compile
# path's setting; batch 7's question 1, answered (a) on 2026-09-27 (POSITIONS.md, the
# numerics plans), bounds an unbounded type parameter by Any, and under it the switch-over
# takes that bound for the compiled path (CLIMB-BATCH-7.md section 1, Q1), so the 372
# "bound Object" errors of the plain compile setting are the setting's, not the library's
